claims.explanation: Triangle G B3 B5 is not equilateral. The angle at B3 subtends the 60° arc GB5, so it is 30°, not 60°.
The angle at B5 subtends the diameter GB3, a 180° arc, so it is 90°, not 60°.
This is not an interior angle of the regular pentagon. The angle at B5 between B5G and B5A3 subtends the 216° arc GA3 not containing B5, so it is 108°, not 36°.
This is the same angle at B5 as the previous one, so it cannot be 60°. Its actual value is 108°.
Since G2 lies on line GB3, ray GG2 is the same as ray GB3. Therefore this angle equals angle B3GB5, which is 60°, not 36°; the alternate-segment theorem does not apply here.
G, B3, and G2 are collinear, with G2 on the extension of GB3 past B3. Therefore angle GB3G2 is 180°, not 84°.
G2 lies on the ray B5A3, so this angle equals angle A3B5G, which is 108°, not 60°.
The angle at B1 in triangle GB1A2 is 108°, not 72°: it subtends the 216° arc GA2 not containing B1.
The angle at A2 is 30°, not 36°: it subtends the 60° arc B1G not containing A2.
The angle at G1 between G1G and G1B5 is not 72°; the actual line directions give about 21.6°.
The line GB5 is perpendicular to B5G1, so this angle is 90°, not 60°.
This angle is at G1, and it is not 48°; it is about 21.6°. The preceding step computed an angle at G, not this angle at G1.
The angle between G2G and G2B5 is 12°, not 36°, because B5, A3, and G2 are collinear and that line makes a 12° angle with the horizontal line GB3.

claims.quoted_text: The difference between these two angles gives us \( \angle G G_{2} G_{1} = 12^{\circ} \).
claims.explanation: You cannot subtract angles at two different vertices, one at G1 and one at G2, to obtain the angle at G2. The final numerical value happens to be 12°, but this derivation is not valid.
